big: A share at ₹300 earns ₹15 a year. A bank share trades at ₹210 against ₹100 of net worth. A share at 30 times earnings grows 30% a year. Four multiples, four ways to put a price next to something real.

lines: It depends on the business. P/E compares price with earnings. EV/EBITDA compares the whole business, debt included, with operating profit. P/B suits banks. PEG divides P/E by expected growth, so a P/E of 30 with 30% growth gives one.

h: P/E from the same price, made up
alt: Bars comparing P/E and EPS for two shares at the same price
caps: A trades at 20 times, B at 60 times.

q: A share priced at ₹300 earns ₹15 a year. What is the P/E?
why: 15 is the EPS. It does not answer what was asked.
300 is the price. The details here point elsewhere.
4,500 multiplies, which is wrong. That does not match this case.
300 ÷ 15 is 20. That matches the case described.

q: A bank share trades at ₹210 against ₹100 of net worth per share. What is the P/B?
A share at 30 times earnings grows earnings 30% a year. What is its PEG?
why: 30 ÷ 30 is 1. That matches the case described.
30 is the P/E. It does not fit the facts given.
0.3 divides wrongly. It does not answer what was asked.
900 multiplies, which is wrong. The details here point elsewhere.

q: Two companies carry different debt loads. Which multiple compares whole-business value against core profit?
why: P/B compares price with net worth. It does not fit the facts given.
PEG adds growth to P/E. It does not answer what was asked.
EV includes debt, so it handles different debt loads.
Dividend yield is a payout ratio. That does not match this case.

pts: P/E = price ÷ EPS. P/B = price ÷ net worth per share.
EV/EBITDA compares the whole business with operating profit.
